name: Victor Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Brennan Electrical, which is two vans and three of us, in a small town where everyone knows your mum. Most days I'm rewiring old terraced houses, swapping out fuse boards from the eighties, chasing cables into plaster that crumbles if you look at it. I like the fault calls best, when a whole kitchen's dead and you find the one burnt connector. What wears me out is the crawling under floorboards and the boss's paperwork, which he still does on carbon pads.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the money side look like for you right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, tight. I'm on the lower end of pay for a sparky, and I live with Hanna, my partner, in a flat above the bakery on Station Road. She works nights at the care home, and between us we cover rent and bills and that's about it. I've got maybe three or four hundred in the bank, and there's only one other electrical firm within twenty miles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype? I'd believe that. I've never touched any of those AI apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. In the canteen at the builders' merchant everyone's been on about AI for two years and none of it's ever pulled a cable through a joist. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the union group chat, something about the robots still needing us to plug them in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't mean I'm safe, it just means the old problems stay. Pat, my boss, is sixty-three and talks about packing in every winter. If he sells up and the other firm doesn't want me, I'm driving an hour each way or I'm out of the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, I'm not the type to go chasing new things. I'd try to get Pat to put in writing what happens to the vans and the customer list if he retires. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, though I've said that before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a relief and a weight at the same time. Relief that nobody's coming for my job with a computer. But the weight is that my life still sits on one old man's knees holding out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fifty a month. What usually stops that from happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something always breaks. Last month it was the tyres on my own car, two hundred and forty quid, and the month before Hanna's phone screen. The fifty goes first, every time, before the takeaway on Friday even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Pat did retire, what would you actually do the next week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Hughes, the other firm, the same morning, cap in hand. If they said no, I'd sign on with an agency doing new-build work out by the ring road. I'd hate it, it's all first fix in cold shells, but rent doesn't wait.

say: I'd tell everyone I **told them so**, because AI never pulled a cable through a joist.
I'd post a **sarcastic joke** in the union group chat about robots needing us to plug them in.
think: My real worry is **Pat retiring**, not AI, because he's sixty-three and talks about stopping every winter.
With **one other firm** in twenty miles, losing this job means a long drive or leaving the trade.
do: Keep doing the **same rewires** and fault calls with the firm.
Ask Pat to **put in writing** what happens to the vans and customers if he retires.
Try to save **fifty a month**, even though repairs have eaten it before.
feel: **Relief** that no computer is coming for the job.
A steady **weight** from depending on one ageing boss and almost no savings.
S0.quote: My life still sits on one old man's knees holding out.
fieldNote: Even with nothing changing, his **thin cushion** and an ageing boss keep him worried.
He's **proud** of never touching AI apps and enjoys being proved right.
Savings plans **collapse** at the first repair bill, like the tyres and the phone screen.
His **fallback** is ringing the one rival firm, then agency new-build work he'd hate.

steps.text: Keep rewiring old houses and taking fault calls for the firm
Put fifty pounds a month into savings before Friday takeaway

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and booking and that. Not much of that in my day, apart from Pat's carbon pads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's the office people who should worry, not us. I'd be telling the lads at the merchant's that you can't email a socket onto a wall. Online I'd be sharing the union stuff about protecting jobs, because some people are going to get hurt by this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it gets at us sideways. If the people in offices lose their jobs, they stop getting their kitchens redone, and our work dries up. And if Pat sells, whoever buys the firm will want everything booked through some app, and I'm useless with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the work. I'd go to the union branch meeting for once, the one in the pub back room, because they'll know what's coming before I do. And I'd stop the Friday takeaways and the streaming, because if work slows I need every pound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit stupid, if I'm honest. Everyone keeps saying learn the apps, and I just don't want to. It feels like being told to change who I am to keep a job I'm already good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should carry the cost of the people who get hurt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies making a fortune off it, plain and simple. If a firm swaps ten office staff for software, it should pay into something that retrains them or keeps them going. I'd vote for whoever says that and actually means it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Say a new owner wants all jobs booked and invoiced through an app. What do you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably get Hanna to show me, she's better with phones than me. I'd do the bare minimum on it and grumble the whole time. If it was really bad, I'd ask the union if they can make the firm give proper training on paid time.

say: I'd say **office workers** should worry, because you can't email a socket onto a wall.
I'd share **union posts** online about protecting people who get hurt by this.
think: Office **job losses** mean fewer kitchen and house refits, so work dries up for us sideways.
A new owner would want **app bookings**, and I'm useless with that kind of thing.
do: Go to the **union branch meeting** in the pub back room to hear what's coming.
Cancel **takeaways and streaming** so every pound is there if work slows.
feel: **Uneasy**, and a bit stupid for not wanting to learn the apps.
**Resentful** at being told to change who he is to keep a job he's good at.
S1.quote: Everyone keeps saying learn the apps, and I just don't want to.
fieldNote: He sees the **indirect hit**: office workers with less money stop paying for refits.
His resistance is **open and admitted**, not hidden behind talk of being fine.
He wants **companies to pay** for the people they replace, and would vote that way.
Would lean on his **partner** and the union rather than learn the booking apps himself.

steps.text: Attend the union branch meeting at the pub this month
Cancel the streaming subscription and the Friday takeaway
Vote for a party that makes firms pay for replaced workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before my van's MOT runs out twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a government with a spine. I'd be the one in the group chat saying don't let them roll this out without rules. To friends I'd say we're hands-on, we've got a bit longer than the office lot, but not by much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me. The thinking stuff comes for Pat's side first, the quotes and the regulations and the testing certificates. Then three years later a robot that can chase a cable into crumbly plaster turns up, and I'm thirty with no savings and nothing else I know how to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join every union action going, the rallies, the letters, all of it. I'd try to get on the waiting list for the council housing association, because I can't see us keeping up rent if Hanna's care home brings in robots too. And honestly, I'd probably just keep working till someone tells me to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like standing on a pier when the tide's coming in fast. I don't have a plan, and two years isn't long enough to make one with three hundred quid in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Hanna's job might change too. What would that mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Care work is half lifting and half paperwork and pills. If the paperwork side goes to AI first, they'll cut her hours, and her nights are what keeps the rent paid. If both of us lose a third of our money in the same year, we're moving back to my mum's spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in that three-year gap between the thinking AI and the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's when I'd be busiest, maybe, because people panic and rewire for all the new gadgets. But I'd be working for whoever owns the software, at whatever rate it decides. I'd be earning the money to watch my own replacement get built.

say: I'd demand **unions and rules** before anyone rolls this out.
I'd tell friends **hands-on work** buys a little longer than office jobs, but not by much.
think: The **quotes and certificates** go first, then robots arrive while I'm thirty with nothing else.
A robot that can **chase cable** into crumbly plaster is the one that ends my trade.
do: Join **every union action**, from rallies to letters, as soon as it's announced.
Get on the **housing association list** in case both incomes drop.
Keep working **day to day** until someone tells him to stop.
feel: **Sick**, like standing on a pier as the tide comes in fast.
**Helpless**, with no plan and only a few hundred pounds saved.
S2.quote: I'd be earning the money to watch my own replacement get built.
fieldNote: He understands the **three-year gap** well: busy at first, then replaced by robots.
Household risk doubles because his partner's **care home** could cut her paperwork-heavy hours.
Fallback is **moving in** with his mum, which he says flatly rather than angrily.
Lots of protest energy, but **no personal plan** beyond keeping working.

steps.text: Join the union's rallies and letter campaigns against unregulated rollout
Put their names on the housing association waiting list
Keep taking every rewire and fault call while work lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, rules first, but I'd sound less panicked. I'd tell the lads that five years is time to make the government do something, so let's actually do it this time. Online I'd be pushing for a tax on firms that swap people for machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years to AGI and eight to the robots means I'd be thirty-five when it lands on me properly. That's too old to start again from nothing and too young to retire. I think I'd just be dragged along, because I don't jump early, I never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still not learn the AI stuff, I know that about myself. I'd do the inspection and testing course, the one that lets you sign off other people's work, because a robot still needs a human signature for a while. And I'd stand for the union branch committee, which I've always said no to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but there's a bit of fight in it. With five years I can at least see the shape of the thing. It's still my life being decided by people in glass towers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the testing course, when you don't want to learn the apps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's still the trade, it's still a meter and a screwdriver and the rulebook. I trust that. Someone has to be legally on the hook when a house burns down, and I reckon that stays a person for longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for it with so little saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The union has a learning fund that covers some of it, and I'd ask Pat to chip in, since it helps the firm too. I'd do it on Saturdays. Hanna would grumble because Saturday's our only day together.

say: I'd use **five years** to push the government into acting, and say so loudly.
I'd campaign online for a **tax on firms** that replace people with machines.
think: At **thirty-five** I'd be too old to start fresh and too young to retire.
I don't jump early, so I'd likely be **dragged along** by events.
do: Take the **inspection and testing course** on Saturdays, part-funded by the union.
Stand for the **branch committee** after years of saying no.
Keep **refusing AI tools**, knowing that's who he is.
feel: **Worried**, but with some fight now that the change is visible.
**Resentful** that his life is decided by people in glass towers.
S3.quote: Someone has to be legally on the hook when a house burns down, and I reckon that stays a person for longer.
fieldNote: The extra years turn panic into **campaigning** rather than personal adaptation.
He'd retrain only **within the trade**, picking inspection work that keeps a human signature.
Money for the course depends on the **union learning fund** and his boss.
Still expects to **lose the trade** around thirty-five, so worry stays high.

steps.text: Enrol on the inspection and testing course on Saturdays
Stand for the union branch committee this year
Campaign online for a tax on firms that replace workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Right, I'd be thirty-seven before AGI and forty before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so no excuses for the government this time. To the lads I'd say there's time to get the apprentices sorted and make sure the rules say a human signs off every board. I'd still be the sceptic in the room, but a calmer one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough that I'd probably end up running something for Pat, or for whoever buys him out. I'd still be scared of the robots at forty, but forty with some savings is different from twenty-seven with none. I just don't trust myself to actually save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the testing course, slower, over a couple of years. I'd push Hanna and me to set up a proper standing order, a hundred a month into a separate account I can't see. And I'd keep going to the union, because ten years of pressure could actually change the law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but it's the normal sort of anxious. The kind I have about rent anyway. It feels like something I could plan for, even if I'm bad at planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust yourself to save. What would make it stick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Taking it out before I see it, the day the wages land. And Hanna holding the card. If it's in my current account, it's tyres or a round at the pub, I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing at forty, if the robots do arrive then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to be the one checking the robot's work and signing the certificate. Or teaching at the college, because someone has to teach the old way so people know what's safe. I wouldn't want to be on the dole watching a machine in my old customers' lofts.

say: I'd say a **decade** leaves the government no excuse for doing nothing.
I'd push for rules so a **human signs off** every fuse board.
think: Ten years means I could end up **running the firm** for Pat or a buyer.
Forty with **some savings** feels different, though I don't trust myself to save.
do: Do the **testing course** slowly over a couple of years.
Set up a **hundred a month** standing order into an account he can't see.
Keep going to the **union** to press for changes in the law.
feel: **Anxious**, but the ordinary kind he already has about rent.
**Able to plan**, even though he admits planning isn't his strength.
S4.quote: I wouldn't want to be on the dole watching a machine in my old customers' lofts.
fieldNote: A decade makes the threat feel like **ordinary rent worry** rather than terror.
He knows his **saving habits** fail and builds a rule to stop himself spending.
Dreams of being the **human signature** or a college teacher, still within the trade.
His thin cushion and **few local jobs** keep him from feeling truly calm.

steps.text: Spread the inspection and testing course over two years
Set up a hundred-a-month standing order the day wages land
Keep attending union meetings to press for sign-off rules

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years with three hundred quid and a boss about to retire is nothing. What would help is the union having real teeth, and some kind of support that keeps tradespeople in the trade while the rules get written, like paid retraining that doesn't come out of my weekends.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the partners. Everyone asks me about my job, but Hanna's nights at the care home are half our rent. If you only look at one of us, you miss how close we are to my mum's spare room.

headlineQuote: If you only look at one of us, you miss how close we are to my mum's spare room.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old electrician** at a three-person firm, rewiring old terraced houses in a small town.
He lives with his partner above a bakery, with **a few hundred pounds** saved and one rival firm nearby.
He has **never used AI** and is proud of it, preferring the meter, the screwdriver and the rulebook.
He moves from **anxious to alarmed** as AGI speeds up, and answers with union action, not personal change.
Given time, he'd retrain only **inside the trade**, aiming to be the human who signs off the work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years with almost no savings and a retiring boss leaves no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **union with teeth** and paid retraining that keeps tradespeople in the trade without eating weekends.
Support that counts the **whole household**, since his partner's care-home wages pay half the rent.
